question_text: A 8-month-old girl is brought to her pediatrician because her mom is concerned that she may have a "lazy eye". She was born prematurely at 33 weeks and was 3 pounds at birth. Her mother also says that there is a history of visual problems that run in the family, which is why she wanted to make sure that her daughter was evaluated early. On presentation, she is found to have eyes that are misaligned both horizontally and vertically. Physical examination and labs reveal no underlying disorders, and the patient is discharged with occlusion therapy to help correct the misalignment. Which of the following would most likely have also been seen on physical exam?

                    ### Question
                    A 8-month-old girl is brought to her pediatrician because her mom is concerned that she may have a "lazy eye". She was born prematurely at 33 weeks and was 3 pounds at birth. Her mother also says that there is a history of visual problems that run in the family, which is why she wanted to make sure that her daughter was evaluated early. On presentation, she is found to have eyes that are misaligned both horizontally and vertically. Physical examination and labs reveal no underlying disorders, and the patient is discharged with occlusion therapy to help correct the misalignment. Which of the following would most likely have also been seen on physical exam?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Asymmetric corneal light reflex
opb. Bitemporal hemianopsia
opc. Increased intraocular pressure
opd. Fundus neovascularization
ope. Nystagmus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 8-month-old girl with misaligned eyes is likely experiencing strabismus, which is characterized by misalignment of the eyes. A common finding in strabismus is an asymmetric corneal light reflex, indicating a deviation in eye alignment. The possibility of bitemporal hemianopsia is unlikely in this case, as it typically suggests a neurological issue, which has not been indicated by the examination. Increased intraocular pressure is also unlikely given the absence of underlying disorders. While the history of premature birth raises concern for retinopathy of prematurity, fundus neovascularization is not a direct finding associated with strabismus itself. Nystagmus can occur in conjunction with strabismus, but it is not universally present. Therefore, the most likely finding on physical exam, supported by consensus, is an asymmetric corneal light reflex.
